newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Think-tank urges Hungary to stop real wages fall.
newsitem.headline: Think-tank urges Hungary to stop real wages fall.

text.p: A prominent Hungarian think-tank said on Thursday that the disappointing economic growth this year should make the government prevent a further drop in real wages to increase consumption.

Deputy chief executive of the Kopint-Datorg Rt think-tank, Andras Koves, told a news conference that gross domestic product (GDP) could grow by 0.5 to one percent in 1996 and two percent in 1997 -- in line with government forecasts.
But to achieve this the government must stop a two-year decline in real wages and household consumption, by meeting its ambitious inflation targets next year.
"If this trend (falling real wages) will continue for a long time, this may threaten the improvement of in the balances (of payments and budget) which has already been achieved," he said.

Kopint-Datorg said the government helped the business sector to become more profitable in 1995 and 1996, but it was disappointing that enterprises, discouraged by low domestic demand, were not increasing investment.
"Among 1996 economic processes, perhaps investments show the most worrying picture," the think-tank said in a statement.
Kopint-Datorg forecasts investment to increase by three percent this year, while household consumption would decrease by two to three percent after a drop of six percent in 1995.
The think-tank said real wages were likely to drop by five to six percent in 1996 compared with the two percent fall planned by the government.
This was because inflation would drop from last year's 28.2 percent only to 23-24 percent in 1996 and not 20 percent as targeted.
Koves said the government should calculate inflation for 1997 more carefully to prevent a further drop in real wages.
He was sceptical about the government's 1997 inflation target of 18 percent, saying he saw consumer price growth in the 19 to 21 percent range.
The think-tank expects Hungary's imports to increase six to seven percent next year, while exports should grow nine to 10 percent.
He said higher exports would not be enough to boost GDP growth substantially.

But if real wages preserved their real value in 1997 while consumption was cut by only five to six percent instead of the planned 10 percent, investments could increase by five to six percent and the GDP would grow by two percent.
